title: Better, Not Perfect: Why a Public Message Needs a Prototype, Not a Poster
subtitle: A policy paper can be perfect and still fail in a lobby. The wording is argued over in committee, signed off, translated, printed — and then the first visitor walks in, stops four metres from the panel, reads nothing, and leaves. None of that is a copywriting problem. It is the height of the sign, the direction of the queue, the first question on the form, the object nobody wants to pick up. Design has known this for a century: version one is not a draft to be hidden, it is the instrument that tells you what the real thing is. deTour's theme this year is 'BETTER, NOT PERFECT: Prototypes for Tomorrow' — the prototype is honest in a way no finished deck can be. Public communication is close to the last discipline still sending finished work to its first rehearsal. What follows is not an argument for lowering the standard. It is an argument for testing in the room before you print.

title: Play as Policy: Why Gamified Civic Education Works
subtitle: A statute is an abstraction, and abstractions do not survive a shopping mall. That is the design problem facing every civic education campaign: the content is fixed, serious and often dry, and the audience is a family with a pram and ninety seconds to spare. The instinct is to explain harder — bigger panels, more text, clearer diagrams. The evidence points somewhere else. When people are given something to operate — a flight stick, a maze, a claw, a role — they learn more, and they keep more of it, than when they are simply told. What follows is not an argument for making public messages trivial. It is an argument for making them operable — and not merely entertaining: across 77 studies, games beat ordinary instruction on what people retain, without making them any more motivated. The fun is not the mechanism. The doing is.

title: Not Louder, Better Designed: Where a Message Becomes a Feeling
subtitle: People do not remember what they were told. They remember what they did. A programme can put its message on every screen in the city and still leave the room untouched, because information travels easily and experience does not. The work that changes behaviour is narrower and harder: building a moment a person chooses to step into — something to touch, solve, carry away or stand inside — so that the point behind the policy arrives as a feeling rather than a sentence. That is the difference between announcing a message and staging it, and unlike volume it can be measured. The three numbers below are what that difference looks like once someone finally counts it.
